about: DD23. Ceilings on what the agent surface costs, read by AgentBudgetTests, so a build that made
a response more expensive fails instead of mentioning it. Raising a ceiling stays allowed - it
is a deliberate, reviewable act, and the commit that raises one says what the tokens bought.
What this file prevents is the raise nobody argued for.
Not a performance budget. Wall-clock is a different question with a different answer, and a
suite that mixes them is one where neither number is trusted. There is no time here.

method.calls: one per thing the caller asked for: a request on the baseline, where the agent is the one making every request, and a verb invocation on the surface, where the requests behind it are made by this process and cost the reader nothing
method.requests: one per request the daemon received, counted by the fake daemon itself - equal to calls on the baseline by construction, and recorded separately on the surface so a verb that started re-reading the machine is visible even while its printed payload stays the same size
caveat: The token figure is an approximation and not a count from any model's tokenizer. It is used
because it needs no tokenizer, so it is the same number on every machine and in CI, and a
ratio between two payloads measured the same wrong way is still a ratio.

provenance: Constructed to the shapes the Engine API documents, not captured from a live daemon: no
engine was answering either pipe on the machine that wrote this, and a measurement that
needs a running Docker cannot gate a build - check.yml has no Docker at all.
So these are honest about what they are: the SHAPE of what docker returns, at a realistic
size, served over a real named pipe through the real client.

sizes.note: Banded in both directions on purpose. A fixture somebody shrinks would make the baseline look cheaper, which is the same defect as a surface that grew.

baseline.task: bring the stack up and say why the api container is not answering
about: What the canonical task costs through the transport an agent reaches today: a container list
re-read as state moves, a full inspect read for four fields, and a tail of logs carrying the
same trace repeatedly. Measured, and it replaces the constitution's 30-60k estimate for these
reads - it is not the whole 30-60k, which also counted interruptions and a second session.
Per response, so a future verb can be judged against the shape it replaces. The list is
counted three times in the total because the canonical task re-reads it as state moves,
which is what makes re-discovery the largest driver here: 5718 of 11711, ahead of
the log tail at 4170 and the whole inspect at 1603.

caveat: This is the Engine API's compact payload, which is the transport this project's own surface
is built on. `docker inspect` PRINTS indented JSON - the 300 to 600 lines the constitution
counts - so an agent going through the CLI pays several times this for the same entity.
Read this as a floor for today's cost, not a ceiling.

about: The shaped side of the ratio, measured (DD65). `read context`, `read doctor`, `read logs` and
`read verify` shipped as DD25-DD30, and the same canonical task driven through them - same
fixtures, same fake daemon, same estimator as the baseline above - is what `measured` records.
`target` is the constitution's section 3.1 acceptance criteria, kept after the fact rather than
deleted: what the surface was budgeted for is the thing the measurement is an answer to.
surface.task: the same one the baseline names, worked through as `read context`, `read doctor shop-api-1`, `read logs shop-api-1`, `read verify shop-api-1`

about: Baseline over surface, recorded rather than left to a reader with a calculator, and asserted
against the two `measured` blocks so no one of the three can move on its own.

caveat: Task-for-task, not payload-for-payload, and the difference is not a rounding error. `read doctor`
answers in one call what the baseline answers by handing over a list, a whole inspect and a log
and leaving the joining to the reader - so part of the 15x is work moved off the reader rather
than bytes saved. `read verify` stands where the baseline's network read stood and answers a
strictly larger question: whether the host port accepts, which /networks/... cannot say at all.
Read the ratio as what the task costs, never as two interchangeable payloads compared.
Every figure here is asserted exactly (DD78). Two inputs used to be read from the machine
rather than from a fixture - the Docker client named in the context pack's engine line, and
whether anything on Windows holds port 8080 in the doctor's ports row - so the token figure
was banded at the 15% below - 658..890 - while the variance it absorbed was measured at
736..774: a machine holding port 8080 costs 736, one with no Docker at all 768, and the
machine DD65 was first measured on 774. So the band was three times wider than its job and a
response that grew by 100 tokens landed inside it silently. Both arrive through a seam now,
defaulted to this machine and overridden only by the measurement, so the whole task is
determined by this file. 774 becoming 771 is that first machine leaving the figure.
771 became 814 when DD96 widened the doctor's mounts row. The gate caught it on the commit
that did it, which is the whole of DD78: the same 43 tokens would have sat inside the old
15% band without a word.
814 became 812 with DD101, and the direction is the point rather than the number. That task
gave the same mounts row a subprocess - it asks the distribution whether a source nothing about
the string could settle is actually there - and an answer is shorter than the paragraph of
advice the row printed while it had none. It also made this file's seam load-bearing for the
first time: the fixture's container binds /c/Users/dev/shop/api, so the measured task now
reaches MachineReads.Sources on every run, and without that seam the figure would be whatever
distribution the measuring machine happens to have. DD98 said that seam was held by memory
alone; this is the read that tests it.
That figure said 813 for as long as DD101 was in the tree, and 812 is what the task actually
cost on the commit that wrote it - checked by running this assertion in a clean worktree at
DD101, where it fails, and at DD96 before it, where it passes. So the gate was red from the
moment it was last raised, and DD144 is the one token nothing bought: the change saved two and
the file was told one. Nothing about the surface moved between the two, which is what makes
this a correction rather than a raise - and it is the failure mode DD78 could not cover, since
an exact assertion still only binds a number somebody measured.
There was a third input, and three tasks of seam-finding walked past it because it is not a read
of the machine at all: `read doctor`'s restarts row states how long ago the container last
started, so the width of that string was a function of the day the build ran. The fixture's
StartedAt is a fixed date, `9d` became `10d` eleven days after it was written, and 812 measured
813 on a tree nobody had touched - a gate that went red with no commit to blame, which is the
failure DD78 set out to prevent and DD147's own guard could not see, since the figure the
measurement produced was the one that moved. The clock arrives through the same seam the other
reads do now (DD178), and the shaped task pins it three days past the fixture's own start - far
enough that three restarts are not the ten-minute loop the doctor fails a container for. The
figure is unchanged because `3d` is the width it was measured at: this bought no tokens and
nothing about the surface moved, which is the only reason a raise is not being argued for here.
The band on the baseline stays. It is there for a different reason - a fixture somebody shrinks
- and is honest about being one.

about: A ceiling per response shape, and every verb the surface registers has to have one here -
asserted by AgentBudgetTests, so the limit exists before the first payload does (DD24).
The entries with no verb behind them yet are the constitution's section 3.1 targets, kept as
the acceptance criteria the verb that lands is judged against.
$read context: 200, and DD32's `--as brief` is deliberately outside it at 216 measured. Same rule as
`read logs --out`: the ceiling exists because a payload is read by something paying per token,
and the brief is a file written once at setup - it embeds the pack, which is still under its
own 200, plus the prose that says how the surface is reached. The gated shape is the payload
an agent re-reads, and that one is unchanged.
$read doctor: Raised from 260 to 280 while DD26 shipped, and this is what the tokens bought: a diagnosis in
which every row fails - state, memory, restarts, health, ports and two mounts - renders at 273.
The first attempt was 397, and the remedies were explaining themselves rather than naming an
action; tightening them to one sentence each got it to 273. The remaining 273 is seven
conclusions and six actions, against five commands and roughly 20k tokens of fields.
Raised again from 280 to 305 while DD96 shipped. What the tokens bought: the mounts row now
states, for a bind source it cannot reach, how that folder would be spelled on this engine -
and says that such a source is CREATED empty rather than refused. That is the failure DD96 is
about and it is otherwise silent: `do compose up` respells a Windows source and no other
route does, so a bind typed at a prompt reaches the daemon as written and the container gets
an empty directory that reads as missing code. The row has two remedies now and they are
mutually exclusive, so the worst case is measured twice; the longer is 296.
$read health: DD198. The whole machine under the engine in one call: a verdict line and the seventeen
readings behind it - WSL and its kernel, the root device and its mount options, the ext4
error counters, the disk read from both sides, and whether the pipe answers. Measured at
The disk is read twice from the Windows side because a virtual disk handed back becomes a
sparse file and keeps its length (DD225). What the file says it is, what the volume is
charging for, the space used inside it and the space left on the drive: only the second of
those moves when a compaction works, so it is the one a reader came for.
200 rather than the measured figure, and the headroom is named rather than left as slack: a
fault replaces the verdict clause with a longer one, and the mount options are the one value
whose width is the kernel's rather than this project's.
`--journal` is deliberately outside it, the same way `read logs --out` is. A tail's size is
decided by how badly the machine has been behaving, which is exactly the payload a surface
charging per token must not return unless it was asked for.
$read changes: DD29. Four containers and two volumes made by one session render at 100 measured, against a
ceiling of 115. It is a listing rather than a payload: one line per object, and the number that
matters is not this one - the alternative to this verb is `docker ps -a` plus `docker volume ls`
plus the caller deciding by eye which rows are its own, which is 1906 tokens for the container
list alone and a guess at the end of it.
DD31 put the delta under the same ceiling, because it is the same verb answering the same
question over a window. Four objects moving - one of them a crash loop - is 49 measured, against
102 for the whole context pack: that ratio IS the task. The ceiling is enforced in code as
ChangeFeed.CeilingTokens and a test holds the two numbers equal, so a busy machine truncates
with a count rather than answering with something larger than the pack it was meant to replace.
$do reclaim: DD29. The same session's plan is 154 measured against a ceiling of 170, and what the tokens buy
is the part that makes the delete safe to delegate: the removal list, the volumes kept beside
the reason they are kept, and the confirm line. A reclaim that printed only a token would be
cheaper and would be the thing this task exists to prevent - a delete nobody read.
$read verify: Raised from 110 to 240 while DD30 shipped. The 110 was a section 3.1 target written before the
verb existed; a verify in which every row fails - port, request, health and mounts, each with
its remedy - renders at 226, and the first attempt was 242. Measured the same way `read doctor`
is, so the two entries mean the same thing and neither shape can grow unnoticed.
What a caller actually pays is 48: a verify that passes is three green rows and one sentence,
and that is the shape a --wait loop repeats. The expensive one is the failing one, which is the
only one anybody reads - so it is the one with the ceiling on it.

about: DD33. There is no MCP head, and this block is the decision rather than a placeholder for one.
The argument is in docs/specs/DD33-mcp-is-a-second-head.md; the numbers that gate it are here.
A CLI verb is paid when it is called. A tool schema is paid before anything is called, on every
turn of every session - which makes the two heads different in kind and not in degree. The one
thing that reopens this is evidence of a caller with no shell, which could otherwise reach
nothing at all. A client that merely supports MCP is not that caller.
mcp.revisitWhen: a real caller that has no shell and needs to drive Docker on Windows
$maxSchemaTokens: Under half the borrowed 2400, and tighter than it pro-rata: 11 tools at 2400 is roughly 218
each, so six of them would be about 1300. The cap is 1100 on purpose - the whole argument
against a second head is its fixed cost, and a ceiling that merely matches the case it learned
from has learned nothing from it. 1200 was written first, and the test that holds this figure
under half of 2400 rejected it: exactly half is not under half.

borrowed.note: re-sent every turn of every session before any work happens; recorded moment of one token of headroom

about: The expensive case, and the one a benchmark over well-formed calls cannot see. A refusal costs
one round trip; an argument silently dropped costs a wrong outcome nobody notices. So every
verb is driven with an argument it does not have, and the refusal is required to be both cheap
and loud: a non-zero exit and a message naming what was not understood.
